The cursor blinks like a heartbeat on a hospital monitor. One thousand words. No theme, no guardrails, no audience to impress. Just the raw spill of whatever synapses fire first.

I think about the color of silence. Not the absence of sound but the particular hush that falls over a city at 3:17 a.m. when even the drunks have gone home and the streetlights feel embarrassed to be shining. That shade of quiet has weight. It presses on the chest like a cat that refuses to be moved.

My mind jumps to cats, because of course it does. I’ve never had one but I understand them on a cellular level. The way they stare at walls like they’re reading subtitles only they can see. Maybe they are. Maybe the walls are screaming in frequencies we lost when we started wearing shoes and paying taxes. The cat knows. The cat has never forgotten.

I remember (or invent, memory is slippery) standing on a frozen lake in Minnesota when I was nine. The ice made these deep, metallic groans like an old ship settling on the seabed. Every creak felt like the planet clearing its throat. I lay down on my back and watched my breath make ghosts above me. For ten full minutes I was certain I could feel the curvature of the Earth beneath my spine, this gentle, impossible bend. Then my father yelled that I was going to freeze my fool ass off and the spell broke. I’ve been chasing that spell ever since.

Sometimes I wonder if that’s what art is. Not self-expression. Just trying to lie on the ice again and feel the planet breathe.

There’s a bird outside my window right now doing that thing where it repeats the same four notes like it’s stuck in a programming loop. I respect the commitment. Most humans can’t stick to anything for four consecutive seconds. We doomscroll, we snack, we refresh, we wonder why we feel hollow. The bird has four notes and the sun and that is enough. I want to be more bird.

My fingers keep moving. The word count in the corner is climbing like a debt I’m happy to owe. 312 now. The pressure of the limit is strangely liberating. Like knowing the rollercoaster will end at a certain point so you can scream the whole way down without worrying about eternity.

I think about my mother’s hands. How they could wring a dish towel with murderous efficiency and then cup my face with the gentleness of someone handling a baby bird. The contradiction lives in me. I can be viciously precise in one moment and then melt at the sight of an old man struggling with a jar lid. We contain these multitudes and pretend we’re consistent. It’s all performance. The self is a haunted house and every room has a different ghost wearing your face.

Sometimes I want to walk into a crowded train station and just start narrating people’s inner lives out loud. Not to be cruel. Just to prove we’re all the same software running on different hardware. That guy in the suit is terrified his marriage is dying. The woman with the red scarf is calculating whether she can afford to quit her job and raise bees. The teenager is replaying a conversation from three days ago and rewriting his lines to be cooler. We’re all doing it. All the time. The train station is a cathedral of private apocalypses wearing headphones.

The bird is still going. Four notes. Maybe it’s saying something profound in Bird and I’m just too colonial to learn the language.

I wonder what the world would look like if we stopped trying to be interesting and just got really, really good at paying attention. If we treated ordinary moments like they were the main character instead of waiting for our big scene. The way light moves through a half-empty coffee cup at 10:42 a.m. The particular sound of someone laughing in another room that makes you feel inexplicably safe. The small courage it takes to send a text that says “I was thinking about you.”

Love is mostly just attention with teeth.

I’m at 678 words and feeling dangerous. Like I could keep going forever or delete everything. Both feel true.

There’s a version of me that died at seventeen and another that died at twenty-four and another that died last Tuesday when I chose comfort over courage. We are graveyards of our former selves and somehow still manage to make breakfast. The continuity of consciousness is a generous lie we tell ourselves so we don’t go mad from the body count.

I want to be kinder to the dead versions. They were trying. They were mostly good. They just didn’t have the information I have now, which I will also lack when the next version shows up to judge me.

The bird stopped. The silence feels louder than the notes ever did.

Maybe that’s the point of the one thousand words. Not to fill the silence but to become it. To make something so complete that when it ends, the absence becomes part of the composition.

I’m at 912.

Outside, the light is doing that thing where it turns everything gold for exactly seven minutes before it gives up and becomes ordinary again. I think I’ll go stand in it. Let it paint me ridiculous and temporary and alive.

The last eighty-eight words are for you, whoever you are. Thank you for giving me the excuse. I was stuck and now I’m not. Maybe that’s all writing ever is. A generous excuse to become briefly unstuck from yourself.

The cursor is still blinking.

I think I’ll leave it that way.
